en: Having prostrated before the sole cause of all, who is the ornament upon the crests of the faces of Brahmā and Rudra, this instruction on the Siddhānta is set forth.
The definition of the words of the Vedas, which is beyond ordinary characteristics, is being set forth by Śrīnivāsamakhin;
in matters of censuring or praising the earth, it excels even the rule of constant application (*nityayoga*).
"And when there is the manifestation of a combination [of phonemes], the possessive suffixes *matup* and so forth occur"—
having thus reflected upon these ancient instructions (*pūrvaśikṣās*) and the *Prātiśākhyas* in their entirety,
I shall now expound the *Siddhānta-śikṣā* in accordance with the Vedic commentaries.
The sequence of examples for words beginning with 'a' and so forth shall be presented there in order—at the beginning, middle, and end—as far as the Veda extends.
This [example] has never been brought forward before; indeed, it was not a sacrificial oblation (havis) previously.
Indra did not slay Vṛtra while he was giving to another;
nor does he drive away this Vṛtra, for you shall eat first. "From this further standing place, come toward us with your aids," so it is also said. 6–7.

May he obtain the rays of light in the forest; may he not be deprived of his offspring by those who act with violence as before; and if he has previously attained greatness, may this [protection] beginning with the letter 'a' reach him.
May there be well-being for you from the wind that follows the bird.
The one beyond created the waterless cup and the water; he who is without deceit and whose name ends in 'a', the one who flows together, has cast away the barley.
Even the one who chose first, speaking over the others, has warded it off.

The word *anta* (end) [is used] even when it is not fixed (*aniṅgye*), and [the suffix] *naṅ* occurs even when followed by *paraśu*; [the word] *arcat* [is used] with *dūmān*, and *juhavām* follows *veḥ* in the sense of running (*dravaṇe*).

The word *vara* is preceded by *āha* here, and [the suffix] *ya* occurs after *deva* even in the case of *āyāma*. *antodānte'pyaniṅgye ca paraśaunaṅpare'pi ca* *arcandūmāca juhavāṃ veḥ paraṃ dravaṇe param* *varāhapūrvamihataṃ devepyāyāmayānti ca* (Note: This is a verse from the *Śiśupālavadha*, Canto 16, verses 84–85, which describes the grammatical rules of Pāṇini in poetic form.)
If a word ending in "a" that is not a finite verb (atiṅ) is accented on its final syllable and is praised, [it is called pragṛhya].
Also, *sadanam*, *ṛtasthāḥ*, *asthavit*, and *astaṃ* [are pragṛhya] when they appear at the end of a hemistich (*parārdha*).
Furthermore, *mṛtyuḥ*, *avaipetaṃ*, and *tadantī* are [pragṛhya] when placed here [at the end of a hemistich]. 12–13.
Now I shall explain the [sacrificial] materials beginning with the *āghāra*, preceded by the *avadāna* (cutting-off);
for this purpose, the root *tap* should not be used with the prefix *ā*.
When one says "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) comes into the forest" or "I am coming," it is in the context of the *vadānaka* (the act of cutting).
The words *skhalaya*, *acāpa*, *de*, *pādāya*, *asaṃśravasi*, and *pāuke* [are used];

the four vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, and *e* are always placed after [the preceding consonant] when they lack a specific color (quality); the word *eva* ends in a long vowel; and the prefix *niṣ* is preceded by *pari*. 15–16.
For the sake of the sacrifice, those who have not previously offered oblations and are now imploring [you] praise you;
come to our sacrificial grass, O Agni, and let the meters be present before you.
(17) After the letter *r*, when preceded by a consonant, the vowel *i* sometimes follows.
A short vowel may occur when the letter *ya* follows immediately after it (in the same word). However, in words such as *lakṣmīya*, the *yaṇ*-substitution does not take place;
in that case, even though there is a word boundary, the established form is *triyambakam*.
In the *Kāṭhaka*, there are also [the mantras] beginning with *bhartryo*, *ya tryo*, *rātrya*, *pitryam*, and *āmantrya*;
furthermore, the words *patnī*, *asvaḥ*, *dhiṣṇya*, and *tanvām* occur when joined with a semivowel substitute (*yaṇādeśa*).
Also [the mantras] *saṃjñānam asi*, *loko 'si*, *tubhyam bhadram*, and *saha*.
These five have been proclaimed by the ancients and are declared to be the Kāṭhakas.
There are eight known as the Kāṭhakas:
Hotrī, Naptrī, Śatārudrī, and Varyasī, which exist in two forms.

*kriṣṭidhrī* and *strī* end in long vowels; those following [the previous] consist of a single short syllable. *chinnaṃ*, *pratisatāṃ*, *śikyaḥ*, *śamyo*, and *goṣvabhilipya* [end in long vowels]. *pṛśchidaṃ* stands in three places; *sumati* and *tam̐hajīrṇaṃ* [are examples]. *parājiha* [ends in a long vowel].
May I contemplate; may I contemplate: he sleeps, he does not move. 24.
Begged, he quickly [went] with speed, he who is without speed, crossing over;
having spread out the sacrificial grass, he conquered the goat, and the conqueror made the sound of victory. 25.
"Yield milk through faith; she who has lain down shall lie down again.
By these [verses], the Virāj was first indicated in this section (prapāṭhaka). 26.
The year is eightfold—neither will it roar nor will it rain; [these are] the purificatory waters."
Those who are dear cause such great pain here;
may you, O most gracious one, by the Eternal Law, rise up at night as the foremost Sarasvatī, like Mitra, for our protection; may the voice of the beloved one flow forth with joy.
Agni indeed is the one who shaves the hair for the gods;
he should also possess the sound "iri" in the *anuvākas* beginning with "rakṣām̐si.
[The formulas] "Sarasvati," "priyebhyaḥ," "hi," "śucike," and "to hiraṇyayoḥ" [are likewise included]. 29.
"He makes light for me; may that which is yours prosper"—this is the sixteenth [verse].
"May you be such a one," [he says] regarding the pole; though the two [axles] are placed there, they move forward even while she looks on, and he waits without waiting. 31.
Thus, one should first be an Agnihotrin; even a female buffalo, when she is pregnant with a leopard cub, gives birth to offspring that are full-grown.
[The word] *dhāvateḥ* begins with the letter *pra* and the vowel *u*; it also follows after the word *iṣṭakā*.
He places the vow upon this earth as food; the one who follows is superior. 33. He sprinkles, he sprinkles with nourishments; he sprinkles those who eat the foam.
From this, the short [vowel] becomes one without a breach; but the subsequent [syllable] is a seat by chance. 34.
O Yudhma and Yuva, you two are truly fierce; though being urged on, you have not followed after [the enemy].
The *kurīra* ornaments shone brightly, pure, with the well-sounding *prasuta*.
If the word *vatsa* does not precede it, and the letter *d* is followed by *au*, even when *upa* follows. 35.

May he who dwells among the drugha, asthānu, āsippi, and siṣu, and among those who lie down (śayeṣu)—may he protect us from those who sleep soundly, from the sorcerers (yātujūnām), and from the kuluñcas, even though they have beautiful feet;
may Kuluṅga, Asnuk, and Sujihva [protect us] from those who lack kin (vibandhuṣu). 36–37.
*didyutaḥ*, *babhlu*, and *karuṇam*; *bāhū*, *uru*, and *suṣuvuḥ*; *madam*, *śutudriḥ*, *gauravitam*, and *ca*; *gugupset*, *tṛpṇutaḥ*, and *bhuvah*.
(38) [The augment] *pu* occurs before the three preceding roots (*śo*, *so*, *do*) and after the following roots (*śaṣ*, *ha*, *sa*).
The *svarabhakti* (vowel fraction) occurs after the letter *r* followed by the vowel *u*; it does not exist [after *r*] followed by another vowel. [Examples:
*bhāgyam*, *parastanu*, *mo ṣū*, *carma*, *dho*, *ndratamūdimaḥ*, *agnāviṣṇū*, *kratū syātām*, *ūrjo bhāgam*, *śatakratau*. 39–40.

This *ṛṣabha* (the bull) belongs to him whose two parts begin with the syllable *ṛ*; it is supreme, consisting of *kvala* fruits, and its life-force is above; it is a triplet (*ṛca*) visible to one who moves forward. 41.
May he support us and may he nourish us; may those who have acted treacherously toward the three-footed [sacrifice] be struck down.
Before the vowels *a* and *ā*, one places the vowel *ṛ* for the four *hotṛ*s (42). But there, [the words] beginning with *ekāra* are *etaṃ*, *etat*, *śreṇa*, *etya*, *neṣi*, *ca*,
*mṛtyuṃ*, *yaje*, *prayati*, *ahve*, *te*, *yajñe*, *śreṣṭha*, and *vatsare* (43).
O Citra, Kirmīra, Kalmāṣa, Śabala, and Etā,
you shall reach even the variegated [realm] of the Daityas through the Soma, Indra, and Traividya weapons; O gentle ones, you proceed toward the deep Soma, which is the arrival of the Asuras.
*pūtudraudhāṃ pare praukṣatān kena puruṣaṃ paraḥ* (45) *auhanta paurṇamāsassyādantodāttaśca kevalaḥ*.
Thus ends the first chapter.
The word beginning with *ka* is desired in the sense of "desiring" (*kamiṣyante*); it is superior to this world.
From the root *kaṭ*, they say *kaḍ* refers to that which is fashioned all around by the two Aśvins (46).
[The words] *āśātikā*, *arbha*, *kāra*, *namaḥ*, *vṛtti*, and *suvṛktayaḥ* [are also derived from *ka*].
Having sprinkled the blood of the hero, purified by its separation from the putrid, she who is called the one who turns back what is stuck, having given birth, she cuts through with her blade;
she is the well-yoked chariot-pole of the Eternal Order, and she is also known as Maḍṛk. 47–48.

He dug a trench of *khadira* wood, a six-branched one; he who eats with his hooves, who is harsh, the burrower, the forest-dweller, and the clawed one—those who find pleasure in digging and being dug—he [overcame].
(49) He is the pit of Mitra, the famous one; he goes to the pit, the female who goes, the seer, and the remedy.
"Niguto gupyate gardānavagadgāmayeti ca" (50);
"jagārapalitaḥ prāk cedājagandhavidīga yaḥ maināge rājagān rugṇaphaliṅgaṃ vaṃsa godhvagat" (51).

As the sinless one, having ascended the mountain peak of Kulunga and having gone to the bed of Jiga, he, free from sin, went forth with his horses; then, with his steeds, he went to the mountain where the waters flow, and Maghavan, whose arrows are not in vain, struck down the enemy who was like a devouring serpent.
With the nose they desire to strike, or by means of food they have increased their sin; 53.
From there, moving toward the skin, hitherward, all around, crosswise, and in various directions, they are always bowed down;
they sigh, they choose, and they take hold of the auspicious; likewise, join yourselves with *vṛṅ*, *dhṛṅ*, and *hiṅ*. 54.

From here, even from the west, you have brought back the sacrificial piling and the hymns of speech; you have fashioned the song of unison. May the divine animal, with its single *chayati* and its share of the second part, protect you.
He conquers, he is conquered; having conquered, he grows old, he consumes the prize of victory.
56. He offers oblations for the singer; he leaps for the sake of victory; he breaks down what is unsubdued;
he is attached, the two most straight paths; one should anoint them; the forward-directed ones pass over; by speed, one wins through victory. 57.
May the two who bestow strength, the wise ones, the Kaṭhodalas, with waters above, bring forth the leafy abundance; may the sixfold one, fashioned from clay,
together with the two, dwell in the house of the one who contemplates the beloved as supreme.
Because the letter *ta* is established here, it moves, desires, and protects (59).
Having brought it to rest, one should enjoy it at the end; thus, after that, the Creator of the universe, dwelling in the heart, desires to give and impels the vital breath (60).
You act straightforwardly, you act as the seventh, you act as the host; then you provoke, you cause distress, you torment, you oppress, you deceive, and you are the one who clings closely.
61. That which was uttered by the Brahman, consuming it, he has swallowed up.
Let the *daṇḍa* (staff) and the *vidatya* (dice-board) be cast aside; let us play with the *śodana* and the *vibhīdaka* nuts.
62 Place the first, the lowest, and the highest [dice] upon the gaming board; O Dhava, blow them forth!
As the Kavya bird flies toward the stars, so may the new ones be gathered back into the *ṛjīṣa*. 63

The letter *pa* becomes long when followed by *pipat*, and likewise when followed by *nasaṃpara*. In the passage "sauparṇaṃ pipato chidre," one expects *apaplā*. The syllable *praṇītām* is not [part of] the word *āpaḥ*; [the forms] *yakṣma* and *prapata* are *saṃsṛpau*.
O Hero, drink the soma;
choose for yourself the abundance of wealth. Shine forth with splendor, O Lord of the house, like a beloved bridegroom.
May the swift bond be broken; quickly let Rebha and Śarabha be freed from their bonds.
The word *mimānaḥ* would be udātta on its first syllable; [the words] *jīvān*, *naḥ*, *manmabhiḥ*, *tamaḥ*, *samanā*, and *samane*; two words each beginning with *puṭa* and ending with *śata*;
and *brahma*—in these cases, when followed by a word ending in the suffix *-maya*, such as *hiraṇmayaḥ*. (67)

In the *yajus* formulas, when *ijyu*, *bhaye*, *jyāyāḥ*, *sakadhyārthau*, and words ending in a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel are followed by *tyajyam*, *ityā*, *nyajuṃbhye*, and *ca*, there is elision; likewise after *rūn*, *mām*, *rayasomayā*, *sārṣṭi*, *sarjati*, and the *varga* [group], as well as before *hrādau* and *urukam*. 68. Before *prayam*.
In the sacrifice, Karikrada, Asaradan, Vatsya, Avayantrita, Jlaplakṣaya, Daśloṇat, Babhluśa, Hlāda, and Malmala—these did not remain steadfast; tell me, O Vanjanā, what did they attain? 69–70.
The gods chose you for the state of following your footstep; through your power, those possessing the *vakāra* uttered crooked speech, and they have indeed flowed away.
O pure one, the swift horse of the merchant hastens toward the rustling of the forest.
"O Meṣī, you are indeed equal to that [Lord] through the power of His command;
O Mahisāhī, some who were bewildered have been severed from their delusions by this name.
Thus spoke Ananta, the Supreme Lord, in order to cut away the infinite doubts of his followers. 72–73.
Seventy-four verses have been uttered by Śrīnivāsādhvarīndra, the moon to the four lineages, in this *Siddhāntaśikṣā*.
Thus ends the *Siddhāntaśikṣā*.
